Abstract: Flaky tests are tests that pass or fail non-deterministically. They may succeed in one run and fail in another without any change in the code. In addition, flaky tests make it difficult to detect real regressions. This paper presents ATRA (Advanced Test Report Analyzer), a framework designed to analyze and visualize historical Cucumber BDD test results. The framework automatically collects test results from multiple historical runs stored in a Git repository. It then processes and classifies each test scenario based on its behavior across runs. ATRA categorizes scenarios into four classes: Consistently Failing, Flaky, New Failure, and Consistently Passing. This classification helps Quality Engineers (QEs) quickly understand the health of the test suite. The framework provides an interactive interface where QEs can select a time window of historical runs for analysis. ATRA then generates comparative reports that include trend line graphs and status distribution pie charts. These visualizations help engineers identify unstable tests and observe failure trends over time. In addition, ATRA allows QEs to record investigation notes directly within the framework. These notes are automatically committed back to the Git repository, creating a traceable history of test analysis and debugging activities.

Abstract: With behavior-driven development (BDD), domain experts describe system behavior and desired outcomes through natural language-like sentences, e.g., using the Gherkin language. Abstract: Domain Specific Languages (DSLs) provide a means of unambiguously expressing concepts in a particular domain. Abstract: User stories are widely used in agile software engineering as a lightweight requirement artifact, but they are rarely sufficient as a single input for producing reliable test artifacts. Ambiguity, incomplete context, inconsistent backlog labels, and limited acceptance information constrain the direct transformation from user stories to test cases. This paper presents a systematic literature review that maps research patterns, gaps, and design implications for an agentic large language model framework supporting user story-to-test case transformation. The retrieval process used a 2016-2026 publication window and was executed across ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and SpringerLink to cover major software engineering and computing venues. The search returned 361 initial records. After duplicate removal, title and abstract screening, retrieval checking, and full-text eligibility assessment, 42 studies were retained for the final corpus of the narrative-thematic synthesis. The synthesis indicates that user story-based test generation requires context enrichment through acceptance criteria, backlog information, requirement text, technical artifacts, and validation feedback. The reviewed studies also indicate a shift from rule-based, model-based, natural language processing, and behavior-driven development approaches toward large language model-based generation, retrieval-augmented generation, schema-aware prompting, validation loops, and multi-agent orchestration. Unlike broader reviews on LLM-based software testing or requirements-based test generation, this review isolates the agile user-story-to-test-case transformation path and derives an agentic design model in which requirement identification, context enrichment, test artifact generation, validation, and traceability checking are treated as separate but coordinated responsibilities within a role-based multi-agent workflow.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-powered assistants are increasingly used for generating program code and unit tests, but their application in acceptance testing remains underexplored.
